subject: korean
title: Which draft will the senior say yes to?
goal: Judge four draft requests by their wording and explain which features make a request easy to grant and which polite-looking drafts still fail.
thinking: Comparing drafts against evidence in the wording
Separating politeness level from effectiveness
Explaining a judgement
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to turn a command into a polite form. Here every draft is already 'polite' in some way, and you must judge which is likely to work and why.
prerequisites: Has seen -(으)ㄹ 수 있을까요 in requests
material:
You are a university first-year. 민준 선배 is a club senior, three years older; you have spoken to him only twice. He took good notes in last week's lecture. Your exam is tomorrow afternoon and you want to see the notes today. You wrote four draft messages:

Draft A: 선배, 지난주 필기 보내 줘요. 내일 시험이에요.
Draft B: 선배님, 혹시 지난주 필기를 사진으로 보내 주실 수 있을까요? 내일 시험이라서요.
Draft C: 선배님, 바쁘시겠지만 시간 되실 때 아무 때나 지난주 필기를 보여 주시면 정말 감사하겠습니다.
Draft D: 선배님, 필기 보내 주세요. 안 보내 주시면 저 시험 망해요.

steps.prompt: Judging only from the wording, which draft is most likely to get a willing 'yes' in time?
hints: Compare who each draft sounds like it is written to.
Ask of each draft: does it give the senior a comfortable way to say no, and does he learn when you need it?

options.text: Draft B
options.reveals: You noticed a question form that leaves room for a no, together with a reason and a time pressure.

options.text: Draft A
options.reveals: This one sounds like talk between close friends or a command; the speaker has noticed the exam but not the relationship.

options.text: Draft C
options.reveals: You rated politeness highly; check whether a very polite message also tells the reader how soon it is needed.

options.text: Draft D
options.reveals: Honorific endings are present, but the second sentence pushes responsibility onto the senior. Check how it feels to receive.

steps.explain: Draft B asks whether it is possible (혹시 + -(으)ㄹ 수 있을까요), gives a reason, and the reason shows the time pressure. Draft C is very respectful but never says it is needed tomorrow, so the senior may answer next week. Draft A has no honorific closeness for a distant senior, and Draft D pressures him.

acceptable.reason: Only B combines a softened question, a reason, and a visible deadline.

steps.prompt: In 2-3 sentences (English or Korean) explain: (1) which words in Draft B make it a request rather than an order, and (2) why Draft C, although very polite, may still not get you the notes in time.
hints: Quote the exact Korean words from Draft B that you mean.
For part 2, imagine you are the senior and read Draft C: what do you not know?

checks.label: names a softening feature of Draft B
connects Draft C to missing time pressure

selfAssess: Did I quote Korean words from the draft, not only say 'it is polite'?
Did I explain the problem with C from the senior's point of view?
Could another reader tell my two points apart?

modelAnswers.text: The ending -(으)ㄹ 수 있을까요 and 혹시 turn the request into a question about possibility, so the senior can decline easily, and 시험이라서요 gives the reason. Draft C never says tomorrow, so he cannot tell it is urgent and may reply next week.

In B the question '보내 주실 수 있을까요?' asks permission instead of ordering. C is respectful, but 'whenever you have time' tells him there is no hurry, which is the opposite of your situation: the deadline is tomorrow.
modelAnswers.note: Focuses on how the reader will read it.

badAnswers.text: Draft C is better because it is more polite.
badAnswers.why: No Korean evidence and no link to the deadline.

steps.humanReview: Whether the learner's explanation really uses the wording (not only the word 'polite') needs a person.

rubric.full: Names Korean expressions in B and links them to easy-to-decline requests
rubric.partial: Says B is polite without naming expressions
rubric.none: Chooses another draft with no wording evidence

rubric.full: Explains that C lacks any signal of the deadline
rubric.partial: Notices C is very polite but cannot say what is missing
rubric.none: Treats politeness level as the only criterion

alternatives: Some learners may rank C first because of the humble 'whenever'; this is acceptable only if they notice the exam is tomorrow (the reveal for c asks them to check).
A learner may write the explanation in English or Korean; both are fine.
hardCases: Draft B without 혹시 would still work; the learner may claim another feature as the main softener.

cautions.language: Korean honorific levels (-세요, -ㅂ니다) and softeners (혹시, -(으)ㄹ 수 있을까요) are shown in context. The checks accept English or Korean explanations.
cautions.culture: Seniors and juniors in clubs differ in status even at small age gaps; this is typical in Korean universities but not in every culture.
cautions.accessibility: Drafts are plain text and can be read by screen readers; no images or colour cues.

auto: Choice of the key; presence of a Korean softener or a deadline remark in the explanation
human: Quality and accuracy of the explanation

subject: korean
title: Say no to a senior, then to a friend
goal: Find the register slip in a refusal to a senior, then rewrite the refusal for a close friend while keeping thanks, a reason and an open door.
thinking: Evaluating a draft for register and promises
Adapting the same message to a different audience
Combining thanks, reason and an open door
differsFromPlain: Plain practice drills -ㄹ 수 없어요 patterns. Here you must spot why a nearly-correct refusal is wrong for its audience and rewrite it for another.
prerequisites: Knows the difference between 존댓말 and 반말
Knows how to say you cannot do something (못, -ㄹ 수 없다)
material: Both 김 선배 (a club senior, five years older) and your close friend 지아 (same age) have invited you to events on Saturday evening. You have a family dinner that evening. This is your draft refusal to the senior:

steps.prompt: One line of the draft to 김 선배 does not fit the audience. Which line?
hints: Read how each line ends and ask which one would sound out of place addressed to someone five years older.
Ask what a senior hears when you promise something for the future.
lines: 토요일에는 가족 저녁 약속이 있어서 못 갈 것 같습니다.
다음에는 제가 꼭 가겠다고 약속할게, 선배!
steps.explain: Line 4 switches to casual speech (약속할게, 선배!) towards a senior and promises more than you can control. Lines 1-3 keep honorific endings, thank, give a reason and decline softly.

steps.prompt: Now write the refusal to your close friend 지아 (same age; casual speech is fine). Thank her, give the reason, and leave the door open. 2-3 short sentences in Korean.
hints: Lines 1-3 of the senior draft thank, give a reason and decline. Do those three jobs in friend-style words, then add a fourth: leave the door open.
Keep it warm: say what you regret, not only what you cannot do.

checks.label: gives a reason or says you cannot go

selfAssess: Did I do all three jobs: thank, reason, open door?
Is my speech style natural for a close friend of the same age?
Would 지아 feel invited again?

modelAnswers.text: 초대해 줘서 고마워! 그날 가족 모임이 있어서 못 갈 것 같아. 다음에는 꼭 같이 가자.
와, 불러 줘서 고마워. 아쉽지만 토요일엔 약속이 있어서 안 될 것 같아. 담에 또 불러 줘!
modelAnswers.note: Uses casual 반말 and the shortened 담에.

badAnswers.why: No thanks, no reason, no open door.
Gives a rude reason instead of a real one.

badAnswers.text: 고마워. 가족 저녁이 있어서 못 가. 다음엔 나 부르지 마.
badAnswers.why: Closes the door instead of leaving it open.

steps.humanReview: Whether the tone feels natural for close friends, including slang and endings, needs a person.

rubric.full: Identifies the casual line to the senior and writes the friend version in a consistent friendly style
rubric.partial: Finds the line but the friend version mixes styles

rubric.full: Contains thanks, a reason and an open door
rubric.partial: Contains two of the three

alternatives: Using 해요체 (polite casual) with a friend is also acceptable if friendly and consistent.
Line 3 may sound a little firm, but it keeps the honorific ending; the key still treats line 4 as the register slip.
hardCases: A learner who writes a plausible but unusual reason (e.g. 'my cat is sick') is fine if the key components are present.

cautions.language: Mixing 합쇼체 and 해요체 within a message is usually fine; mixing 반말 into a message to a senior is not.
cautions.culture: Declining invitations without a long excuse may feel abrupt in some cultures, while in Korea a short reason plus an open door is the norm.
cautions.accessibility: Plain text only; no colour cues.

auto: Position of the slip; presence of thanks, reason, open door, no rude wording
human: Naturalness and tone of the friend message

subject: korean
title: Before you say yes
goal: Decide which questions are needed before accepting an invitation, given your own constraints, and write a reply that asks them politely.
thinking: Judging which information is sufficient to decide
Linking personal constraints to questions
Writing a conditional acceptance
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to accept or decline an invitation. Here you must find the missing information first.
prerequisites: Can ask simple questions with 몇 시, 어디, 뭐
material:
Your classmate 하준, whom you have spoken to a few times, sent you this message:

하준: 토요일에 집들이 해요! 우리 집은 학교 앞 서점 옆이에요. 시간 되면 와요~

(집들이 = housewarming party.) What you know about yourself: you work a part-time job until 7:00 p.m. on Saturdays. The last subway home leaves at midnight. You are allergic to shrimp and crab.

steps.prompt: Which questions do you need answered before you can decide whether to go? Choose all that are needed.
hints: For each question, name one of your own facts that would change your decision.
The address is already given, so skip anything the message already answers.

options.text: 몇 시에 시작해요?
options.reveals: You linked your 7 p.m. finish to the start time.

options.text: 집이 몇 평이에요?
options.reveals: The size of the home would not change whether you can go or what you can eat.

options.text: 음식에 새우나 게가 들어가요?
options.reveals: You linked the allergy to the menu.

options.text: 선물은 뭘 사 가면 돼요?
options.reveals: Useful for etiquette, but it does not decide whether you can go; it can be asked after you accept.

options.text: 몇 시쯤 끝나요?
options.reveals: You linked the last subway at midnight to the end time.

options.text: 누가 와요?
options.reveals: Often natural to ask, but none of your listed facts depends on it.

steps.explain: The three facts that could stop you are the 7 p.m. finish (start time), the midnight last subway (end time) and the shrimp/crab allergy (menu). The address is given; gifts, house size and guest list do not change whether you can attend.

acceptable.reason: Asking who is coming is socially natural and does not hurt, even though none of your constraints depends on it.
Asking about a gift is polite and common, though it can wait until after you accept.

steps.prompt: Write your reply to 하준 in Korean (2-4 sentences): thank him, say you may come, and politely ask the questions you chose.
hints: Start with thanks, then give the fact that makes the questions necessary.
Soften the questions with 혹시 or -(으)ㄹ 수 있을까요.

checks.label: asks a question about time (start or end)
asks a question about the food or the allergy

selfAssess: Did my questions match my own constraints?
Is the tone suitable for a classmate I do not know well?
Do I make clear that I may come, not that I cannot?

modelAnswers.text: 초대해 주셔서 감사해요. 저는 7시에 일이 끝나서 조금 늦게 갈 수 있는데, 몇 시에 시작하고 몇 시까지 해요? 그리고 제가 해산물 알레르기가 있는데, 음식에 해산물이 들어가나요?
초대 고마워요! 가고 싶은데 토요일 7시까지 일해서요. 파티가 몇 시까지 해요? 새우 알레르기가 있어서 메뉴도 알려 주실 수 있어요?
modelAnswers.note: Shorter, uses 해요체 and gives facts as reasons.

badAnswers.why: Accepts without checking the facts and asks nothing.

badAnswers.text: 초대 고마워요! 7시까지 일해서 늦을 것 같아요. 새우 알레르기가 있어요.
badAnswers.why: States the facts but asks nothing, so 하준 cannot answer.

steps.humanReview: Whether the questions are natural and polite enough needs a person.

rubric.full: Chooses exactly the questions tied to the three personal facts
rubric.partial: Chooses most but includes one unrelated question

rubric.full: Reply thanks, states the situation and asks the needed questions politely
rubric.partial: Asks questions but without thanks or softening

alternatives: Asking who is coming or about a gift is acceptable (see acceptable sets).
A learner may ask the questions in a different order or with other words.
hardCases: Is the end time really needed? Yes, because of the last subway; a learner who plans to leave early may still reasonably ask.

cautions.language: Learners must form questions; -나요/-ㄹ까요 as well as -어요 are fine.
cautions.culture: Housewarming (집들이) is a Korean custom where guests often bring gifts such as tissue or detergent; allergies may be less often mentioned than in some countries.
cautions.accessibility: The facts are listed in text; no colour cues.

auto: Choice of questions; presence of thanks, a time question and a food question
human: Appropriateness and politeness of the reply

subject: korean
title: The exchange that turned into a refund
goal: Find the line where a customer says the wrong thing at a shop counter and repair the misunderstanding politely.
thinking: Reading a dialogue for inconsistent intent
Locating the source of a misunderstanding
Repairing in polite Korean
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to learn shop vocabulary. Here you track what the customer wants from line to line and must explain why the clerk acts on the wrong request.
prerequisites: Knows 교환 (exchange) and 환불 (refund) as words
material: You bought a jacket yesterday, but the size is too small. At the counter this conversation happens (line numbers start at 1):

steps.prompt: The clerk starts a refund although you wanted an exchange. Which line of the dialogue starts the mix-up?
hints: Write down in one phrase what the customer wants in line 1.
Find the first later line that wants something different.
lines: 손님: 어제 여기서 산 재킷인데요, 사이즈가 작아서 큰 걸로 바꾸고 싶어요.
손님: 영수증은 집에 두고 왔는데, 카드로 계산했어요.
직원: 그럼 카드 내역으로 확인해 볼게요. 사이즈 말고 다른 문제는 없으시죠?
손님: 네, 없어요. 그럼 환불해 주세요.
직원: 네, 환불해 드리겠습니다. 카드 주세요.
steps.explain: Line 5 says 환불해 주세요 although line 1 asks for 큰 걸로 바꾸고 싶어요 (an exchange for a bigger size). Line 6 follows what the clerk heard. Line 3 only says there is no receipt, which can be solved with the card record.

steps.prompt: After line 6 you notice the mix-up. Write what you say to the clerk to repair it (2 sentences, polite Korean).
hints: Say clearly what you did not mean and what you meant.
Soften the correction with a short apology or a reason, then use 교환/바꾸다.
selfAssess: Did I say what I meant, not only what I did not mean?
Is my tone still polite after the error?
Could the clerk now act without asking again?

modelAnswers.text: 죄송해요, 제가 잘못 말했어요. 환불이 아니라 큰 사이즈로 교환하고 싶어요.
아, 아니에요. 환불 말고 바꿔 주세요. 큰 사이즈가 있으면 좋겠어요.

badAnswers.why: Does not signal that the earlier sentence was wrong, so the clerk may not know to stop the refund.

steps.humanReview: Politeness and naturalness of the repair need a person.

rubric.full: Picks line 5 and links it to line 1
rubric.partial: Picks line 6 (the clerk's reaction)
rubric.none: Cannot say which line is inconsistent

rubric.full: Corrects the request, states the exchange, stays polite
rubric.partial: Corrects without politeness or without stating the exchange

alternatives: Some may argue line 6 is also an error by the clerk; it only follows line 5.
Using 바꿔 주세요 or 교환해 주세요 are both fine.
hardCases: A learner may repair with a question ('교환은 안 되나요?'), which is acceptable if it states the exchange.

cautions.language: 교환 and 환불 are different shop words; 바꾸다 is the everyday verb for exchange.
cautions.culture: Receiptless returns with a card record are usual in Korea but shop policies differ.
cautions.accessibility: Dialogue is plain text with line numbers; no images.

auto: Position of the error line; presence of correction signal, exchange wording and polite ending

subject: korean
title: Where do I apply?
goal: Revise your reading of an official's replies as more of the exchange appears, then ask a sensible follow-up question.
thinking: Inferring what an official's indirect reply means
Using times to test a plan
Revising a plan when new conditions appear
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads one official reply and picks the meaning. Here the information arrives in pieces and each piece changes the plan.
prerequisites: Knows 구청 and 주민센터 as offices
material: It is 4:20 p.m. You are at the neighbourhood 주민센터 (community service centre) counter. You want to apply for a passport. You are not sure whether you have your passport photo in your bag.

steps.prompt: Read each part, choose the most likely reading, then continue.
hints: Decide using only what you have read so far.
In stage 2 compute the arrival time before choosing.

stages.info:
나: 저, 여기서 여권 신청할 수 있어요?
직원: 아, 여권은 여기서는 안 되고, 구청 여권과에서 해요.

options.text: This office cannot help you at all
options.reveals: The clerk does help: the reply names where to go.

options.text: Come back tomorrow
options.reveals: There is no mention of tomorrow in the reply.

options.text: Passport applications are handled at another office
options.reveals: You read the place marker 구청 여권과 as a direction.

options.text: Wait here until a clerk is free
options.reveals: No waiting is mentioned.

stages.after: '여기서는 안 되고, 구청 여권과에서 해요' is a refusal for this office plus a direction to the right office.

stages.info: 직원: 구청은 5시까지 접수를 받아요. 지금 4시 20분이죠? 여기서 걸어서 20분쯤 걸려요.

options.text: Leave now and you arrive about 4:40, in time
options.reveals: 20 minutes added to 4:20 gives 4:40, before 5:00.

options.text: It is already too late to apply today
options.reveals: Arrival at 4:40 is before the 5:00 closing.

options.text: You should take a bus because walking takes 20 minutes
options.reveals: The clerk did not say you must take a bus; walking is a fine way to arrive in time.

options.text: The district office has already closed
options.reveals: Closing is at 5:00, still 40 minutes away.

stages.after: The clerk is warning politely that time is limited but enough if you go now.

stages.info: 직원: 아, 사진은 가져오셨어요? 규격 사진이 없으면 접수가 안 돼요. 길 건너에 사진관이 있는데, 거기서 10분이면 찍어요.
stages.ask: With the time left, what is a sensible plan?

options.text: Walk to the district office and check the bag when you get there
options.reveals: If the photo is missing you would have to return, which costs more than 20 minutes.

options.text: Check the bag now; if it is missing, use the shop across the road
options.reveals: You included the contingency: check first, then use the photo shop only if needed.

options.text: Ask this office to accept a phone photo
options.reveals: The clerk said the photo must meet a standard; this office is not the one that accepts it.

options.text: Give up for today and return tomorrow
options.reveals: Photo 10 min plus walk 20 min fits before 5:00, so giving up is unnecessary.

stages.after: If the photo is missing: 4:20 + 10 minutes for the photo + 20 minutes walking leaves you at the office before 5:00.

steps.reflect: Notice how each clause changed the plan: a place, then a deadline you could check with arithmetic, then a condition (photo). Indirect speech from officials often hides the key condition in a short extra sentence.

steps.prompt: Write what you say to the clerk before leaving: thank them and ask one polite question that helps you carry out your plan (2 sentences, Korean).
hints: Which part of your plan are you still unsure about: the road, the photo shop or the time?
Close with a thank-you.
selfAssess: Did I ask about something I really still need to know?
Is the question polite enough for an official?
Would the clerk be able to answer in one sentence?

modelAnswers.text: 감사합니다. 구청까지 어떻게 가면 가장 빨라요?
고맙습니다. 사진관이 어디에 있는지 알려 주실 수 있을까요?

steps.humanReview: Appropriateness of the question for the plan needs a person.

rubric.full: Changes the reading when a new condition appears and checks the times
rubric.partial: Follows the clerk but skips the arithmetic

rubric.full: Thanks and asks a polite, useful question
rubric.partial: Question without thanks

alternatives: Stage 3 admits only the 'check first' plan; another plan may be acceptable if it works within the time.
hardCases: Real offices vary in closing time; the task fixes it at 5:00 to allow the calculation.

cautions.language: Official speech uses -ㅂ니다 and honorific -(으)시; the clerk's remarks are indirect but short.
cautions.culture: Passport applications are handled at specific offices in Korea; other countries differ.
cautions.accessibility: Times are written in words and numbers so a screen reader reads them clearly.

auto: Reasonableness per stage; presence of thanks and a question

subject: korean
title: Two ways to soften a request
goal: Identify which 'softened' sentence is still a command, then write two requests that use different softening strategies.
thinking: Evaluating whether a sentence is really softened
Generating variants with different strategies
Giving a reason as a softener
differsFromPlain: Plain practice changes a command into -세요. Here you test which softening tools actually change how a request feels and then build two on your own.
material:
Situation 1 (a bus on a cold day): the person beside you has opened the window. You are a stranger to them. Four sentences you could say are shown in step 1.

Situation 2 (a library reading room): the person at the next desk is on a speakerphone call. Same age, unknown to you.

steps.prompt: In Situation 1, three of the four sentences are really softened. Which one is still essentially a command?
hints: Ask: could the other person say 'no' to this sentence without it sounding rude?
Compare the four sentences: for each one, decide whether it asks the other person or tells the other person.
lines: 죄송한데 창문을 조금만 닫아 주실 수 있을까요?
혹시 창문 좀 닫아도 될까요? 제가 좀 추워서요.
바람이 좀 차네요. 창문을 닫아도 괜찮으실까요?
steps.explain: Line 3 uses 좀 and -(으)세요, but it is still a command with a reason added afterwards. Lines 1, 2 and 4 open with an apology, a permission question or a remark about the cold and ask rather than tell.

steps.prompt: Situation 2: write TWO different sentences asking the person to lower their voice or take the call outside. Use two different softening strategies, such as an apology opener, a request question or giving your reason. Korean.
hints: Look back at lines 1, 2 and 4 for strategies you could reuse.
Give a reason that is about you, not an accusation.

checks.label: asks as a request (question form or 주시면), not only a command

selfAssess: Are my two sentences different strategies, not the same one reworded?
Would I be comfortable receiving them from a stranger?
Does either sentence sound like an order?

modelAnswers.text: 죄송한데, 혹시 조금만 작게 말씀해 주실 수 있을까요? 제가 시험공부를 하고 있어서요.
실례합니다. 전화 소리가 조금 커서 그런데, 통화는 밖에서 해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
modelAnswers.note: Uses 실례합니다 and a polite request form.

modelAnswers.text: 실례합니다. 제가 책을 읽고 있어서 그런데, 조금만 작게 말씀해 주실 수 있을까요

badAnswers.why: Only a command with 좀; no second sentence, no reason.

badAnswers.text: 죄송한데 조금만 조용히 해 주세요. 죄송한데 밖에서 통화해 주세요.
badAnswers.why: Two apologies but both are commands with the same strategy, and no reason.

badAnswers.text: 죄송한데 밖에서 통화해 주실 수 있을까요? 혹시 조용히 해 주실 수 있을까요?
badAnswers.why: Two requests with the same strategy and no reason.

steps.humanReview: Whether the two sentences really use different strategies needs a person.

rubric.full: Picks line 3 and says why 좀/-세요 does not soften it
rubric.partial: Picks line 3 without reasons

rubric.full: Two sentences with different softeners and a reason
rubric.partial: Two sentences but the same strategy
rubric.none: A single sentence or a command

alternatives: Some may feel line 3 is acceptable between strangers on a bus; the key states it is a command with a reason attached.
Ending with 부탁드립니다 is also a softener.
hardCases: A request with good wording but a blaming reason ('your voice is annoying') may pass the checks but need human review.

cautions.language: 좀 is a softener but never changes the sentence type; the real change comes from asking (-ㄹ까요?) or apologising.
cautions.culture: Directly asking strangers to be quiet is often softened heavily in Korea.
cautions.accessibility: All sentences are plain text; no tone-of-voice cues are required.

auto: Position of the unsoftened line; presence of two sentences, a softener and a reason

subject: korean
title: Why is the clerk confused?
goal: Explain a misunderstanding caused by answering 네 to a negative question and give a reply that cannot be misunderstood.
thinking: Inferring a cause from a short dialogue
Rejecting plausible but wrong explanations
Producing a clear reply
differsFromPlain: Plain practice drills 네/아니요 answers. Here a dialogue shows the answers do not mean what the speaker intended and you must say why.
prerequisites: Can read a short café dialogue
material:
At a café counter:

직원: 여기서 안 드세요?
손님: 네, 여기서 먹고 갈 거예요.
직원: 네? 포장이세요, 아니세요?

The customer wanted to eat inside, the clerk heard something else.

steps.prompt: What most likely caused the clerk's confusion?
hints: Reread the clerk's first question: is it asking about eating here or about not eating here?
Compare the clerk's first question with the first word of the customer's answer: do they point the same way as the rest of the answer?

options.text: 네 can only answer questions about the future, so it did not fit the clerk's question
options.reveals: 네 answers any yes/no question; the question here is about the present. Look at what 네 agrees with.

options.text: The customer's ending -ㄹ 거예요 is too casual for café staff, so the clerk asked again
options.reveals: -ㄹ 거예요 is a normal polite plan ending; the clerk's confusion comes from elsewhere.

options.text: The clerk asked a negative question, so 네 was heard as 'I am not eating here'
options.reveals: You noticed that 네 confirmed the negative question and clashed with the next words.

options.text: The customer said 여기서 where 여기에서 is required, so the place was not understood
options.reveals: 여기서 is the normal short form of 여기에서; the place was clear.

steps.explain: The clerk asked 'You are not eating here?' and 네 means 'that is right', i.e. 'I am not'. Then 'I'll eat here' contradicts it, so the clerk asks again.

steps.prompt: The clerk repeats: 여기서 안 드세요? Write a Korean reply that cannot be misunderstood and shows you will eat inside.
hints: Do not rely on a bare 네 or 아니요; say the full idea.
Mention 여기서 (or 안에서) and an eating verb.
selfAssess: Does my reply state the action, not only 네/아니요?
Does it avoid the possible clash with the clerk's negative question?
Is the ending polite?

modelAnswers.text: 아니요, 여기서 먹을 거예요.
여기서 먹고 갈게요.
저는 안에서 먹을 거예요.

badAnswers.why: A bare 네 repeats the confusion.
Does not say where, so the clash remains.
This is the customer's original reply; starting with 네 repeats the clash.
Still starts with 네 to a negative question.

steps.humanReview: Whether the reply is natural and unambiguous needs a person.

rubric.full: States that 네 confirmed the negative question and clashed with the follow-up
rubric.partial: Says the answer was wrong but not why

rubric.full: Gives a reply that states where you will eat
rubric.partial: Gives a correct but ambiguous reply

alternatives: 아니요, 먹을 거예요 is also a good answer (denying the negative question); both 아니요 and an explicit statement work.
hardCases: Answering a negative question with a bare 아니요 can also be misunderstood; the check only forbids a reply that starts with 네.

cautions.language: In Korean 네/아니요 answer to the statement as asked, not to the facts.
cautions.culture: Customers say 'for here' or 'take out' in English cafes; Korean clerks ask in both directions.
cautions.accessibility: Dialogue is plain text, no sound required.

auto: Key of the cause; presence of 'eating here' wording

subject: korean
title: The Monday that was two Mondays
goal: Find which repair attempts fail to remove the ambiguity and write a repair that cannot be misread.
thinking: Evaluating repairs
Noticing that repeating an ambiguous phrase does not repair it
Writing an unambiguous correction
differsFromPlain: Plain practice drills date words. Here you judge why a repair fails and write one with unambiguous information.
prerequisites: Can read dates written with 일 and 요일
material: Today is Sunday, the 1st. You and your colleague 지수 are making plans. People differ on whether Sunday belongs to this week or the next, so '다음 주 월요일' can mean tomorrow (the 2nd) or the Monday after (the 9th). You meant the 9th. (Line numbers start at 1.)

steps.prompt: Two of your own lines try to repair the misunderstanding but both fail. Pick one of them.
hints: Look at which words the repair uses to name the day.
For each repair, ask what new information it gives 지수 that she did not already have.
lines: 나: 그럼 다음 주 월요일 오후 2시에 만나요.
지수: 네, 그럼 내일 오후 2시에 카페에서 봬요!
나: 아, 내일이 아니라 다음 주 월요일이에요.
지수: 다음 주 월요일이면 내일 아니에요?
나: 아니요, 내일은 이번 주 월요일이고, 제가 말한 건 다음 주 월요일이에요.
steps.explain: Lines 3 and 5 both repeat 다음 주 월요일 / 이번 주 and rely on the very week boundary the two do not share, so they cannot settle the difference. A date (9일) would.

steps.prompt: Write your repair message to 지수 in Korean (2-3 sentences, polite) so that no confusion remains.
hints: Use something that does not depend on who counts weeks differently.
Apologise briefly for the confusion and ask her to confirm.
selfAssess: Does my message contain information that cannot be read two ways?
Did I invite her to confirm?
Is it polite?

modelAnswers.text: 혼란을 드려 죄송해요. 제가 말한 건 9일 월요일이에요. 9일 오후 2시도 괜찮으세요?
아, 헷갈리게 말해서 미안해요. 내일 말고 9일 월요일 오후 2시예요. 괜찮아요?
modelAnswers.note: Names the date and rejects tomorrow.

badAnswers.why: Repeats the ambiguous phrase and gives no date.
Names a date, but the wrong one (5일, not 9일).

steps.humanReview: Tone and naturalness of the repair need a person.

rubric.full: Identifies that repeating 다음 주 does not repair, and explains
rubric.partial: Picks the right line without explaining

rubric.full: Names a date, confirms with 지수, polite
rubric.partial: Names the date without confirmation

alternatives: The key allows line 3 or line 5.
Weekday plus date ('9일 월요일') is the usual repair; 'Monday the 9th' in Korean order is fine.
hardCases: Learners who write '9/9' or 'nine' need the check to be tolerant; the pattern accepts 9일 or 구일 only. A human decides on other formats.

cautions.language: Numbers with 일 (days) are used; the pattern also accepts 월/일.
cautions.culture: Whether the week starts on Sunday or Monday varies; dates avoid the issue.
cautions.accessibility: Plain text, dates written in digits for screen readers.

auto: Position of failed repair lines; presence of a date, apology or confirmation

subject: korean
title: Is that a yes?
goal: Revise a reading of an indirect reply as more of the exchange appears and choose a gracious next move.
thinking: Weighing partial evidence
Revising a judgement as hints build up
Choosing a response that respects the other person
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads one reply as yes or no. Here the answer is gradually revealed and you must change your reading.
prerequisites: Knows 한번 볼게요 and 시간 되면 as phrases
material: You invited a colleague, 지수, to a film on Saturday. She did not answer 'yes' or 'no' directly. Read her replies one by one.

steps.prompt: Read each part, choose the most likely reading, then continue.
hints: Answer only for what you have read so far.
Look at what she does not say.

stages.info:
나: 이번 토요일에 같이 영화 볼래요?
지수: 토요일이요? 음… 한번 볼게요.
stages.ask: What does she most likely mean?

options.text: She has said yes and will come
options.reveals: You treated 한번 볼게요 as an acceptance; later hints may change that.

options.text: She is undecided and hedging
options.reveals: You noticed the pause and the open wording.

options.text: She has clearly said no
options.reveals: There is no clear refusal word.

options.text: She wants a different film
options.reveals: She does not mention any film.

stages.after: At this point it is ambiguous: 한번 볼게요 can mean 'I'll see' and the pause is a signal.

stages.info: 지수: 요즘 좀 바빠서요… 일이 많아서 잘 모르겠어요.

options.text: She is more likely to decline, softly
options.reveals: You used the reason about being busy together with the earlier hesitation.

options.text: She is still likely to say yes
options.reveals: The reason given points towards trouble in coming.

options.text: She wants you to choose the time
options.reveals: She did not ask for a time.

options.text: She is angry
options.reveals: The tone is soft, not angry.

stages.after: Giving a busy reason after hesitating is a typical way to decline without saying no.

stages.info: 지수: 다음에 시간 되면 제가 연락할게요.

options.text: She will contact you tomorrow
options.reveals: There is no day mentioned; 다음에 is vague.

options.text: She is angry with you
options.reveals: Nothing suggests anger.

options.text: A soft no for this Saturday, leaving the next move to her
options.reveals: You combined the hesitation, the busy reason and the vague later.

options.text: She will definitely come on Saturday
options.reveals: She does not say she will come.

stages.after: All three hints point to a soft refusal, though she may also genuinely contact you later.

steps.reflect: Notice that one hedge is weak evidence but three hints in a row (pause, busy reason, vague later) make 'soft no' much more likely than 'yes'.

steps.prompt: What is the best way to reply?
hints: Think about how she can keep face and still feel invited.
Decide whether your reply pressures her.

options.text: 그럼 일요일은 어때요? 그것도 안 되면 말해 줘요.
options.reveals: You offer an alternative day; reasonable but check that it does not pressure her.

options.text: 알겠어요. 바쁘면 어쩔 수 없죠. 시간 될 때 편하게 말해 줘요.
options.reveals: You accept her soft no without pressing.

options.text: 왜 안 돼요? 이유를 말해 줘요.
options.reveals: This demands an explanation she tried to avoid.

options.text: 연락 안 하면 서운할 거예요.
options.reveals: This adds emotional pressure.

steps.explain: A short, relaxed reply respects her soft no and keeps the door open. Offering another day can also be fine if it is light.

acceptable.reason: Offering a different day is acceptable if it is light and you accept a no.

rubric.full: Changes from undecided to soft no and cites the hints
rubric.partial: Reaches the soft no without citing hints

rubric.full: Accepts her soft no while keeping the door open
rubric.partial: Offers another day but is a bit pushy
rubric.none: Presses for a reason or guilt

alternatives: b in the last step is acceptable.
hardCases: She may truly contact you; the task asks for the most likely reading, not certainty.

cautions.language: 한번 볼게요 and 다음에 are vague phrases often used to avoid saying no.
cautions.culture: Indirect refusals are common in Korean and some other cultures; direct refusals may feel impolite.
cautions.accessibility: Dialogue is plain text; no colour cues.

auto: Per-stage reasonableness; key of the reply
human: Whether the learner's rationale matches the hints

subject: korean
title: Wrong dish, right words
goal: Decide what a restaurant owner needs to know and rewrite a blunt complaint as a polite but clear message.
thinking: Selecting needed information
Rewriting for an audience
Balancing politeness with clarity
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks for a complaint sentence. Here you decide what information is needed and rewrite a blunt message for the owner.
material: You ordered 김치찌개 through a delivery app but 된장찌개 arrived. You wrote this blunt message: '음식 틀렸어요. 환불해요.' You will send a new message to the owner (an adult you do not know) through the app chat.

steps.prompt: Which pieces of information will help the owner fix the problem? Choose all that apply.
hints: Think about what the owner needs in order to find and fix this particular order.
Add only what they need to act.

options.text: Which dish you ordered and which one arrived
options.reveals: You identified the core fact of the problem.

options.text: Your complaints about the prices on their menu
options.reveals: This is a different matter and would only bury the real problem.

options.text: What you would like them to do (resend or refund)
options.reveals: You named the outcome so the owner can choose quickly.

options.text: When you placed the order
options.reveals: You included the information that lets them find the order.

options.text: A warning that you will write a bad review
options.reveals: This adds pressure but no information they need to fix the order.

steps.explain: The owner can fix the order if they know what is wrong, which order it is, and what you want. Threats and unrelated complaints do not help.

steps.prompt: Rewrite your blunt message for the owner: say what happened, what you ask for, and be polite (2-3 sentences, Korean).
hints: Start with a greeting or an apology for the trouble.
Replace 환불해요 with a polite question or request.
selfAssess: Did I give facts the owner can act on?
Did I ask rather than order?
Does the message stay calm?

modelAnswers.text: 안녕하세요, 방금 주문한 김치찌개 대신 된장찌개가 왔어요. 번거로우시겠지만 맞는 메뉴로 다시 보내 주실 수 있을까요? 부탁드립니다.
죄송하지만 주문한 음료가 빠져 있었어요. 혹시 환불해 주실 수 있을까요? 감사합니다.
modelAnswers.note: Uses a different problem; same structure.

modelAnswers.text: 안녕하세요. 김치찌개를 시켰는데 된장찌개가 왔어요. 죄송하지만 교환해 주실 수 있을까요?
안녕하세요. 주문한 김치찌개 대신 된장찌개가 도착했습니다. 다시 보내 주시겠어요?

badAnswers.why: Blunt, no softener, no polite request.

steps.humanReview: Naturalness of tone and whether the facts are sufficient need a person.

rubric.full: Chooses the three useful pieces
rubric.partial: Includes one unneeded piece

rubric.full: States the problem, asks politely, stays calm
rubric.partial: Polite but unclear about the problem

alternatives: A learner may choose resend or refund; both are valid requests.
Mentioning the order number is also useful.
hardCases: A message that mentions 'review' neutrally might be flagged by the none-check even though not a threat; human review decides.

cautions.language: Customers usually address owners politely with -시 and -ㅂ니다; 사장님 is a common address.
cautions.culture: Delivery apps with chat to owners are common in Korea.

auto: Choice of information; problem, request, softener and absence of rude wording
human: Tone and sufficiency of the facts
